name: Femoral nerve
summary: The largest branch of the lumbar plexus (L2–L4), the femoral nerve emerges from the lateral border of psoas, passes under the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery (outside the femoral sheath) and divides in the femoral triangle into branches to iliacus, pectineus, sartorius and the four heads of quadriceps and into cutaneous branches for the anterior thigh and, through the saphenous nerve, the medial leg and foot. Its lesions (retroperitoneal hematoma, diabetes, hip surgery, lithotomy position) cause the knee to give way, an absent knee jerk and anteromedial thigh and medial leg numbness.

anatomy.location: Within psoas from L2–L4, emerging at its lateral border to run between psoas and iliacus, beneath the inguinal ligament into the femoral triangle lateral to the femoral artery, dividing within a few centimetres; the saphenous nerve continues through the adductor canal to the medial leg.

subdivisions.name: Muscular branches
subdivisions.note: iliacus and psoas (hip flexion), pectineus, sartorius, quadriceps femoris (knee extension)

subdivisions.name: Saphenous nerve
subdivisions.note: medial leg and foot to the great toe; purely sensory

function: Hip flexion and knee extension; sensation of the anterior thigh and medial leg.

bestView.label: cervical cord; the femoral nerve arises from L2–L4

imaging.normalAppearance: Peripheral nerves of the limbs are outside the MNI brain volume; no atlas mesh is shown. Ultrasound and MR neurography image the nerve directly; electrodiagnosis localizes the lesion functionally. Pelvic CT or MRI reveals a psoas or iliacus hematoma or mass; MRI of the thigh shows quadriceps denervation.

pathology.finding: Hyperdense hematoma within iliacus or psoas in an anticoagulated patient compressing the nerve.

pathology.pathology: Femoral neuropathy after surgery or lithotomy
pathology.finding: Denervation edema of quadriceps with a normal plexus.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: EMG (quadriceps and iliopsoas; adductors spared) and femoral nerve conduction; pelvic CT

lesionEffects.deficit: Knee buckling and difficulty climbing stairs; wasted quadriceps; absent knee jerk

lesionEffects.mechanism: Iliacus involvement (lesion above the inguinal ligament)

lesionEffects.deficit: Numbness of the anterior thigh and medial leg

lesionEffects.mechanism: Obturator nerve intact, distinguishing nerve from L2–L4 root or plexus lesions

examination: Knee extension against resistance and quadriceps bulk
Hip flexion (iliopsoas) to place the lesion above or below the ligament
Hip adduction (obturator) to exclude a plexus or root lesion
pearls: Weak knee extension with an absent knee jerk and normal adduction is the femoral nerve; weak adduction too means L2–L4 roots or the lumbar plexus
Groin pain and quadriceps weakness in an anticoagulated patient: CT the pelvis for a hematoma
